title: Sidecars and exam days: two Korean market quirks explained as the KOSPI slides 4%

Korea's heavy weighting in chipmakers leaves it exposed to any extension of the overnight rotation out of AI-linked stocks, with knock-on effects for regional tech and the won. A weaker won could add to the pressure if foreign investors keep selling. With energy prices elevated by the Middle East conflict, Australia is better placed than many importers, as LNG and coal export earnings help cushion a rising fuel bill. title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6783 – Reuters estimate
body: Earlier this week: China's PBOC lifts FX reserve ratio to 6%: what it means for the yuan, AUD - The People's Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day's closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks.

title: ICYMI: ADNOC denies report of third Hormuz bypass pipeline that could open to other producers
body: A shared bypass line would chip away at the Hormuz risk premium over time by giving Gulf producers beyond the UAE a route to market that avoids the strait. With ADNOC's denial, though, the report is unlikely to move crude near term, and the risk premium stays anchored to shipping attacks and transit volumes through the strait itself. The 2027 second line is the more tangible supply factor, potentially easing Asian buyers' exposure to Hormuz disruption. Repeated attacks on Fujairah also limit how much comfort traders can take from bypass capacity, keeping the infrastructure itself part of the risk. - The pipeline ADNOC says isn't happening would have turned the UAE from a country avoiding Hormuz into one selling a way around it. title: New Zealand Dollar Extends Gains
body: The New Zealand dollar inched up to $0.563 on Thursday, building on gains from the previous session as the US dollar weakened further following a decisive victory by Democrats in the US midterm elections. The outcome reduced fears of a contested result but heightened expectations of political gridlock in Washington, which could constrain President Donald Trump's ability to advance his agenda, including plans for potential new military strikes against Iran. The resulting slide in the US dollar more than offset downward pressure from weaker-than-expected domestic employment data, which led investors to pare back expectations of a Reserve Bank rate hike in December. Markets are now pricing in less than a 50% probability of a rate increase next month, down from about 75% earlier in the week. Investor focus is now shifting to New Zealand's general election on Saturday, with opinion polls pointing to a closely fought contest between the incumbent centre-right National-led coalition and opposition parties led by the centre-left Labour Party. title: BoJ Sees Case for Further Rate Hikes: September Minutes
body: According to minutes from its September meeting, the Bank of Japan judged it appropriate to continue raising interest rates and to recalibrate the degree of monetary accommodation in line with developments in economic activity, prices, and financial conditions. Members agreed that the timing and pace of any further adjustments should depend on the likelihood of achieving the Bank's baseline outlook for growth and inflation, while carefully monitoring risks such as the situation in the Middle East, expanding AI-related demand, and foreign exchange movements. They also underscored the growing importance of anchoring underlying CPI inflation around the 2% target to avoid an excessive overshoot that could damage the economy. One member observed that monetary policy had entered a new phase—shifting from fostering higher underlying inflation to maintaining price stability through flexible responses to changes in domestic and global economic conditions, including exchange-rate-driven price pressures. Capacity pressures remained evident, with a further accumulation of unfinished business. On the price front, both input costs and output charges rose at a slower pace, suggesting some easing in inflationary pressures, even though inflation stayed well above its historical norm. Looking ahead, business confidence slipped to its lowest level since March, as concerns about inflation, population ageing, and persistent labor shortages weighed on the outlook. title: Philippines Inflation Rate Surges to 7.8%
body: The annual inflation rate in the Philippines rose to 7.8% in October 2026 from 7.2% in September, surpassing market expectations of 7.6% and reaching its highest level since February 2023. Transport inflation jumped to 20.1% from 14.6%, while inflation for housing, water, electricity, gas, and other fuels climbed to 9.3% from 8.4%. The ongoing conflict in the Middle East has pushed up energy costs in the Philippines, which is highly dependent on supplies from the region. Price pressures also intensified in several other categories: restaurants and accommodation services (7.7% vs 7%), health (5.9% vs 5.6%), and furnishings and household equipment (5% vs 4.7%). By contrast, inflation for food and non-alcoholic beverages eased to 6.1% from 6.7%. On a monthly basis, consumer prices increased by 0.7% in October, following a 1.0% rise in September. Core inflation accelerated to 5.4%—its highest level since September 2023—from a revised 4.8% in September, also coming in above market expectations of 4.8%. title: Japan Composite PMI Revised Lower
body: Japan's S&P Global Composite PMI Business Activity Index slipped to 52.1 in October 2026, down from both the flash estimate and September's final reading of 52.3. Although this was the lowest level since May, it still signaled an expansion in private-sector activity for the 19th consecutive month. Growth in services activity picked up slightly, but this was more than offset by a slowdown in manufacturing output. Overall new orders rose at the same modest pace as in September, and total sales continued to be supported by stronger export demand. However, growth in new export business eased to a four-month low. On the labor front, employment growth weakened to its slowest pace in a year. At the same time, business confidence regarding activity in the year ahead fell to a three-month low, pointing to a more cautious outlook among firms. In terms of prices, input costs continued to increase sharply by historical standards. However, the rate of inflation in output prices eased to a four-month low, indicating some moderation in firms' price-setting pressures. title: Australia Exports Hit Over 3-Year High
body: Australia's exports rose by 2.3% month-on-month to AUD 48.43 billion in September 2026, the highest level in more than three years, following a downwardly revised 3.1% increase in August. Exports of general merchandise increased 2.9% from the previous month to AUD 42.05 billion. This was largely driven by a 3.6% rise in rural goods exports to AUD 6.4 billion, supported by stronger shipments of meat and meat preparations (up 11.3%) and other rural goods (up 3%). Non-rural goods exports advanced 2.8% to AUD 35.6 billion, reflecting higher shipments of metal ores and minerals (up 2.3%), other mineral fuels (up 6.6%), metals excluding non-monetary gold (up 23.5%), and other manufactured products (up 4.6%). title: Australia Trade Surplus Largest in 7 Months
body: Australia's trade surplus widened sharply to AUD 2.83 billion in September 2026 from a downwardly revised AUD 0.18 billion in August, defying market expectations of an AUD 0.8 billion deficit. This marked the largest surplus since February, driven by rising exports and falling imports. Exports increased 2.3% month-on-month to AUD 48.43 billion in September, a 42‑month high, though the pace eased from a downwardly revised 3.1% rise in August. The increase was led mainly by higher shipments of other mineral fuels and metals. In contrast, imports declined 3.3% month-on-month to AUD 45.61 billion, following an upwardly revised 6.2% gain in August. The pullback was largely due to lower imports of non-monetary gold, civil aircraft, and confidentialised items. The material has been provided by InstaForex Company - www.instaforex.com

title: Australia Imports Fall 3.3% MoM
body: Australia's goods imports declined by 3.3% month-over-month to AUD 45.61 billion in September 2026, reversing a sharply upwardly revised 6.2% increase in August. The fall was broad-based and driven mainly by weaker demand for capital and consumption goods. Capital goods imports fell 2.5% to AUD 12.89 billion, weighed down by a steep drop in civil aircraft and confidentialised items (-33.7%), as well as lower imports of machinery and industrial equipment (-3.7%) and telecommunications equipment (-1.4%). Consumption goods imports also declined, falling 2.2% to AUD 12.54 billion. This reflected reduced purchases of non-industrial transport equipment (-4.0%), food and beverages (-3.6%), and other consumption goods n.e.s. (-0.4%). Imports of non-monetary gold recorded an even sharper contraction, plunging 34.7% to AUD 2.06 billion. By contrast, imports of intermediate and other merchandise goods inched up 0.9% to AUD 18.12 billion, supported by higher inflows of fuels and lubricants (2.3%), parts for transport equipment (2.3%), and processed industrial supplies n.e.s. title: Oil Holds Losses on Hopes for End to Iran War
body: Crude oil traded near $88 per barrel on Thursday, after tumbling more than 8% in the prior session to a one-month low. The sharp selloff followed a Democratic sweep in the US midterm elections, which heightened expectations that the Trump administration could come under growing pressure to wind down the war with Iran. President Donald Trump acknowledged that Republicans suffered electoral setbacks in large part because of the conflict, and he cited rising gasoline prices as a key factor. Still, he signaled no immediate intention to intensify military strikes against Iran. With Democrats now in control of Congress, lawmakers could move to restrict military funding for operations in the Middle East. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer has pledged to press for an end to the conflict. At the same time, crude exports from the Persian Gulf have started to recover, with supply now outstripping near-term demand. As a result, the US crude benchmark is down about 15% so far this week. title: South Korea Posts Record Current Account Surplus
body: South Korea's current account surplus surged to a record USD 61.46 billion in September 2026, up sharply from USD 46.11 billion in August. The goods account surplus expanded to USD 62.75 billion from USD 46.81 billion, as exports soared 92.4% year-on-year to USD 130.72 billion and imports increased 29.4% to USD 67.97 billion. The export boom was driven largely by robust semiconductor shipments amid the global AI upcycle. The primary income account surplus also widened, rising to USD 2.65 billion from USD 1.92 billion, while the secondary income deficit narrowed to USD 0.59 billion from USD 0.94 billion, reflecting a reduction in net secondary income outflows. In contrast, the services account deficit deepened to USD 3.35 billion from USD 1.68 billion, mainly due to larger deficits in the use of intellectual property and other business services. Over the first nine months of 2026, the current account surplus jumped to USD 340.66 billion, compared with USD 89.39 billion in the same period of 2025. title: NZX 50 Hits 2-Month High, Tracking Wall Street Gains
body: The NZX 50 climbed 182 points, or 1.3%, to 13,965 in Thursday morning trade, extending a two-session advance and reaching its highest level since September 4. The move followed overnight gains on Wall Street after the Democrats regained control of Congress. Sentiment was further supported by easing oil prices, which tempered concerns about inflation and further interest-rate hikes amid hopes for a peace deal with Iran. title: Brazil's Central Bank Pauses Rate-Cutting Cycle
body: Brazil's central bank left the benchmark Selic rate unchanged at 13.75% at its November meeting, interrupting its rate-cutting cycle as deteriorating inflation expectations and growing fiscal pressures cloud the policy outlook. Anticipation of looser public spending is pushing inflation projections further above the 3% target. Copom highlighted that the external environment has turned more challenging, with prolonged conflicts in the Middle East lifting oil and refined fuel prices, and monetary policy in advanced economies remaining tight. Domestically, data released since the previous meeting point to a more pronounced slowdown in economic activity, especially in cyclical sectors. The labor market remains resilient but is beginning to show signs of marginal cooling. At the same time, headline inflation and the average of core inflation measures have risen and remain above the upper limit of the target band. title: Oil Slides on Hopes of Iran Peace Deal
body: Crude oil dropped roughly 8% on Wednesday to settle near $88 a barrel, extending its decline for a third straight session and touching a one-month low. Traders increasingly appear to be pricing in an end to the Iran conflict after the White House partially linked Republicans' midterm election losses to the war. Both Washington and Tehran have signaled a willingness to return to talks, with President Donald Trump telling reporters that Iran wants "to make a deal and that could happen." Trump also cited elevated gasoline prices as a factor in the Republican defeat, while Vice President JD Vance publicly blamed the war in a post on X. Qatar continues to mediate between the two sides, and Trump told the Financial Times that the United States has no immediate plans to launch strikes against Iran. At the same time, Democratic control of Congress may limit future military spending in the Middle East, fueling expectations of a near-term peace agreement. On the supply side, fundamentals also pressured prices. A renewal of Gulf exports has pushed the availability of Middle Eastern crude above near-term demand, adding to the downward momentum in the oil market.
